title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
text:
NoteToday



By the end of the class you should be able to

explain in plain words how the spatial scan statistic finds a cluster;
prepare the three input files SaTScan needs and run a purely spatial Poisson scan;
read the output: observed and expected deaths, relative risk, LLR and \(p\)-value;
say what a significant cluster does, and does not, tell us.

The SaTScan background page has more detail and a second worked example.
Packages for today:
Code
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(tigris)                     # county boundaries
library(SpatialEpi)                 # kulldorff()
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
text:
The pattern we start from
The SMR map, with the same classes and colours as your Exercise 4 map: red counties had more deaths than expected, blue fewer, and the palest class is “about as expected”.


Code
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(smr_class = cut(SMR,
                         breaks = c(0, 0.5, 2/3, 0.9, 1/0.9, 1.5, 2, Inf),   # centred on 1
                         labels = c("< 0.50", "0.50-0.67", "0.67-0.90", "0.90-1.11",
                                    "1.11-1.50", "1.50-2.00", "> 2.00")))

# a few counties we will talk about
named <- filter(pa_covid, NAME %in% c("Philadelphia", "Northumberland", "Mifflin",
                                      "Cambria", "Cameron"))

ggplot(pa_covid) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = smr_class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf_label(data = named, aes(label = NAME), size = 2.4,
                fill = alpha("white", 0.6)) +                        # see-through labels
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, drop = FALSE,
                    name = "SMR") +                                     # red = above 1
  labs(title = "COVID-19 deaths, 2020: observed / expected") +
  theme_void()









The highest SMRs are in central Pennsylvania, around Mifflin, its neighbour Juniata and Northumberland, and further west around Cambria. Philadelphia and several of its neighbours are only pale red. Before we run the scan: where do you expect it to find clusters?

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
text:
Idea 1 — A circle that grows
Place a circle on a county centroid. Start with a radius that holds only that county, then let it grow, taking in the next-nearest county each time, until the circle holds a set share of the state’s population: 50% by default. Repeat at every county centroid. A county is inside a circle when its centroid is. Each circle is a candidate cluster.


Code for this figure (optional)
cen   <- st_centroid(st_geometry(pa_covid))
ctr   <- cen[pa_covid$NAME == "Mifflin"]                       # circle centre
d_km  <- as.numeric(st_distance(cen, ctr)) / 1000              # km to centre
ord   <- order(d_km)
share <- cumsum(pa_covid$Population[ord]) / sum(pa_covid$Population)  # population inside
k_max <- max(which(share <= 0.5))                              # largest circle allowed
bb    <- st_bbox(pa_covid)

window_map <- function(k) {
  r_k <- mean(d_km[ord][k:(k + 1)])                            # radius reaching k counties
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = pa_covid, aes(fill = d_km <= r_k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    geom_sf(data = st_buffer(ctr, r_k * 1000), fill = NA, colour = "#D95F02", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_sf(data = cen, size = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey92", `TRUE` = "#FDAE6B"), guide = "none") +
    coord_sf(xlim = bb[c(1, 3)], ylim = bb[c(2, 4)]) +
    labs(title = paste(k, if (k == 1) "county" else "counties"),
         subtitle = sprintf("%.1f%% of the population", 100 * share[k])) +
    theme_void()
}

window_map(1) + window_map(5) + window_map(k_max)









Three of the circles centred on Mifflin. The last one is the largest allowed: it takes in 48 of the 67 counties.

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
section: Idea 2 — Inside versus outside: the likelihood ratio
text:
Idea 2 — Inside versus outside: the likelihood ratio
For each circle, compare the deaths inside with the deaths outside. With the Poisson model the comparison is the log-likelihood ratio (LLR):
\[
\text{LLR} = c \,\log\frac{c}{E} \;+\; (C - c)\,\log\frac{C - c}{C - E}
\qquad \text{if } c > E \text{, otherwise } 0,
\]
where \(c\) is the number of deaths observed inside the circle, \(E\) the number expected inside it at the state rate, and \(C\) the total number of deaths in Pennsylvania. In plain words, the LLR measures how much better the data are explained by a higher rate inside the circle than by one rate everywhere. A circle with no excess gets 0.
We can compute it by hand for five single counties. The code follows the formula letter by letter: c for observed deaths, E for expected deaths, C for the state total.


Code
C <- sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020)                     # total deaths in PA

five <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(NAME %in% c("Philadelphia", "Northumberland", "Mifflin", "Juniata", "Cameron")) |>
  transmute(county = NAME,
            c      = deaths_2020,                  # observed deaths
            E      = E,                            # expected deaths
            excess = c - E,                        # extra deaths
            SMR    = c / E,
            LLR    = if_else(c > E,                # the formula
                             c * log(c / E) + (C - c) * log((C - c) / (C - E)),
                             0)) |>
  arrange(desc(LLR))

Mifflin has the highest SMR in the state, yet Philadelphia, with a much smaller SMR, has the larger LLR. Philadelphia’s excess of about 467 deaths is much harder to explain by chance than Mifflin’s excess of about 61. The scan works with counts, not ratios: a modest excess in a large population can be stronger evidence than a high SMR in a small county. Cameron, with fewer deaths than expected, gets an LLR of 0.
The scan computes the LLR for every circle. The circle with the largest LLR is the most likely cluster.

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
section: Idea 3 — Could the largest LLR be chance? Monte Carlo
text:
Idea 3 — Could the largest LLR be chance? Monte Carlo
Searching thousands of circles, we will always find some circle with a large LLR. The question is whether ours is larger than what a map with no cluster would give. SaTScan answers it by simulation:

Redistribute the 16,030 deaths at random among the counties, in proportion to their expected deaths. This is a map with no cluster.
Run the whole scan on that map, every circle, and keep its largest LLR.
Repeat 999 times.
\(p = \dfrac{\text{number of random maps whose largest LLR} \geq \text{ours} \; + 1}{999 + 1}\)

Because each random map is also searched over every circle, the test already accounts for having looked at thousands of circles. Unlike LISA, there is no need for a separate multiple-testing adjustment.

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
section: Step 1. Write the three input files
text:
Step 1. Write the three input files
SaTScan reads plain text files linked by a location ID. We use the county GEOID.








File
Columns
Here




Case file .cas
location ID, number of cases
GEOID, deaths in 2020


Population file .pop
location ID, year, population
GEOID, 2020, population


Coordinates file .geo
location ID, latitude, longitude
GEOID, county centroid





Code
dir.create("satscan", showWarnings = FALSE)    # folder for the files

# county centroids in latitude / longitude
ll <- pa_covid |>
  st_centroid() |>
  st_transform(4326) |>                         # SaTScan wants lat/long
  st_coordinates()

# one plain table with everything SaTScan needs
ss <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(year = 2020,
         lat  = round(ll[, "Y"], 5),
         lon  = round(ll[, "X"], 5))

# three files, separated by spaces, no header
write_delim(select(ss, GEOID, deaths_2020),      "satscan/pa_covid.cas", col_names = FALSE)
write_delim(select(ss, GEOID, year, Population), "satscan/pa_covid.pop", col_names = FALSE)
write_delim(select(ss, GEOID, lat, lon),         "satscan/pa_covid.geo", col_names = FALSE)

# first three lines of each file
readLines("satscan/pa_covid.cas", n = 3)


[1] "42001 88"   "42003 1009" "42005 69"  


Code
readLines("satscan/pa_covid.pop", n = 3)


[1] "42001 2020 103009"  "42003 2020 1216045" "42005 2020 64735"  


Code
readLines("satscan/pa_covid.geo", n = 3)


[1] "42001 39.87147 -77.2179"  "42003 40.46868 -79.98121"
[3] "42005 40.81193 -79.46461"








WarningTwo common mistakes




The coordinates file lists latitude, then longitude. Swapping them puts Pennsylvania in Antarctica, and SaTScan will still run.
The location IDs must be identical in all three files. A county whose ID does not match is dropped, without an error message.

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
section: Step 2. Set up the analysis in the GUI
text:
Step 2. Set up the analysis in the GUI
Open SaTScan and choose Create New Session.
Input tab

Case File: pa_covid.cas. In the import wizard, map column 1 to Location ID and column 2 to Number of Cases.
Time Precision: None. Study Period: 2020/01/01 to 2020/12/31.
Population File: pa_covid.pop (Location ID, Date/Time, Population).
Coordinates File: pa_covid.geo, Coordinates: Lat/Long.

Analysis tab

Type of analysis: Purely Spatial.
Probability model: Poisson.
Scan for areas with: High Rates.
Advanced, Spatial Window: maximum cluster size 50 percent of the population at risk; window shape circular (elliptic is the alternative for elongated clusters).
Advanced, Inference: 999 Monte Carlo replications.

Output tab

Main results file: satscan/pa_covid_results.txt.
Optional: tick Google Earth (KML) to view the circles, and the shapefile option to map the clusters in R or ArcGIS.

Click Run.

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
section: Where does the p-value come from?
text:
Where does the p-value come from?
kulldorff() keeps the largest LLR of each of the 999 random maps from Idea 3. Plotting them shows the Monte Carlo test at work.


Code
sims <- data.frame(LLR = kd50$simulated.log.lkhd)   # one value per random map

ggplot(sims, aes(x = LLR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tab50$LLR, colour = "red") +      # our clusters
  scale_x_log10() +                                         # values run from 1 to 170
  labs(title = "Largest LLR in 999 random maps (grey) and in our clusters (red)",
       x = "LLR (log scale)", y = "Random maps") +
  theme_minimal()









The largest LLR produced by any random map was 12.4. Every cluster with \(p = 0.001\) lies to the right of all the grey bars: no random map beats it, so \(p = 1/1000\), the smallest value 999 replications can give. A cluster whose red line falls among the grey bars has a larger \(p\)-value.

title: SaTScan in Practice — COVID-19 Deaths in Pennsylvania
text:
Reading the result
The most likely cluster joins 13 counties in the east: Berks, Bucks, Carbon, Delaware, Lackawanna, Lehigh, Luzerne, Monroe, Montgomery, Northampton, Philadelphia, Pike, Schuylkill. Together they hold 44% of the state’s population. They had 8,250 deaths against 7,093 expected: an SMR of only 1.16, or 16% above the state rate, and a relative risk of 1.34 against the rest of Pennsylvania. Yet its LLR, 167.9, is by far the largest. That is Idea 2 again: a modest excess spread over several million people amounts to about 1,157 extra deaths.
Look back at the SMR map: none of these counties is in the darkest classes, and Monroe and Pike are even below 1. They are in the cluster because the circle that captures the large excess around Philadelphia sweeps them in. The cluster’s outline is approximate; its core is what matters.
The relative risk is larger than the SMR because it compares the inside of the circle with the outside, and the outside had fewer deaths than expected. SaTScan reports both.
There is no magic in the LLR. The formula from Idea 2, applied to the cluster’s totals, gives the same value as kulldorff(), up to a small rounding difference inside the package:


Code
c_in <- kd50$most.likely.cluster$number.of.cases    # observed inside
E_in <- kd50$most.likely.cluster$expected.cases     # expected inside
c_in * log(c_in / E_in) + (C - c_in) * log((C - c_in) / (C - E_in))


[1] 168.0353


The secondary clusters are smaller and more intense: Northumberland on its own, a central group around Mifflin and Juniata, and a west-central group around Cambria and Blair, with SMRs between about 1.3 and 2. The last one, Beaver, Lawrence, has \(p =\) 0.045, close to the 0.05 line.
